HQFS, a practical hybrid pipeline that connects forecasting, discrete risk optimization, and auditability in one flow.
HQFS learns next-step return and a volatility proxy using a variational quantum circuit (VQC) with a small classical head.
HQFS converts the risk–return objective and constraints into a QUBO and solves it with quantum annealing when available, while keeping a compatible classical QUBO solver as a fallback for deployment.
HQFS signs each rebalance output using a post-quantum signature so the allocation can be verified later without trusting the runtime environment.
HQFS reduces return prediction error by 7.8% and volatility prediction error by 6.1% versus a tuned classical baseline.
HQFS improves out-of-sample Sharpe by 9.4% and lowers maximum drawdown by 11.7%.
The QUBO solve stage also cuts average solve time by 28% compared to a mixed-integer baseline under the same constraints, while producing fully traceable, signed allocation records.

This study presents a Fourier operator framework inspired by quantum walks that integrates spectral graph theory, Markov processes, and quantum brain dynamics for the discovery of modular structures.
We specifically build Fourier–Markov operators based on quantum walk principles to encapsulate both global frequency components and local transition dynamics of evolving networks.
Our system utilizes superposition and interference effects by mapping random walks into a quantum-inspired Hilbert space, therefore uncovering latent modular structures with enhanced resolution.

The book is structured to provide a progressive learning pathway.
It begins with fundamental concepts such as quantum mechanics principles, qubits, quantum gates, and circuit models.
It then transitions into core quantum algorithms including Shor’s algorithm, Grover’s search algorithm, variational quantum algorithms, and quantum simulation techniques.
Further sections discuss quantum architectures, superconducting qubits, trapped ions, photonic systems, and emerging hybrid quantum-classical computing frameworks.
The final chapters emphasize practical applications in cryptography, optimization, artificial intelligence, materials science, healthcare, and finance.
One of the distinguishing features of this book is its balanced integration of theory and practice.
Mathematical formulations are presented with clarity, while conceptual explanations are supported by diagrams, case studies, and contemporary research developments.
Special attention has been given to recent advancements in Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices and the evolving landscape of quantum cloud platforms.
This collaborative work is designed for postgraduate students, researchers, faculty members, and professionals who seek a structured yet in-depth resource on quantum computing.
It may also serve as a reference text for interdisciplinary programs in computer science, physics, electronics, and information technology.

The successful completion of the book Quantum Computing: Algorithms, Architectures, and Applications is the result of the collective dedication, scholarly commitment, and collaborative spirit of many individuals and institutions.
Their constant encouragement, infrastructural support, and emphasis on academic excellence have significantly contributed to the development of this scholarly work.

We gratefully acknowledge the valuable contributions of all co-authors, whose expertise in quantum algorithms, quantum architectures, computational models, and real-world applications has enriched this volume.

We also express our sincere thanks to peer reviewers and subject experts who provided insightful feedback, constructive suggestions, and critical evaluations that enhanced the quality and coherence of the manuscript.

Special appreciation is extended to our colleagues, research scholars, and students who actively engaged in discussions, experimentation, and knowledge exchange, thereby contributing indirectly to the development of several chapters.
Finally, we extend our deepest gratitude to our families for their unwavering support, patience, and encouragement during the preparation of this book.

codes.code_label: Financial crash estimation in SME networks
codes.text_span: we focus on estimating financial crashes within a network of small and medium enterprises (SMEs) that are customers of Yapi Kredi Bank.
We developed a quadratically constrained quadratic program as a mathematical optimization model aiming at identifying significant vulnerabilities and potential failure points in this network.
The model is inherently nonlinear due to the quadratic terms and constraints, reflecting the real-world complexities of financial networks.

codes.code_label: Quantum computing used to explore solution space
codes.text_span: we leverage quantum computing technology to efficiently explore the solution space and produce decision variables that indicate the likelihood of financial distress for each SME in the network.

The difficulty of this problem lies in the potential domino effect, where a single delayed payment can trigger subsequent financial distress among connected entities, leading to a cascading collapse within the financial network.
Classical computing solutions for such problems would take an impractical amount of time, estimated at 13.7 billion years.
In contrast, using quantum computing, our optimization model solves the problem in approximately 7 seconds.
Using financial data from 2019, our model successfully identified 90.04 million TL out of 107 million TL of non-performing loans.
Similarly, using data from 2020, it identified 669.92 million TL out of 726 million TL of non-performing loans.
Overall, the model accurately predicted 91.2.

Accurately and timely estimating financial crashes are essential for preserving economic stability, achieving risk mitigation, and making informed decisions to safeguard investments and avoid extensive financial crises.

This work extends quantum generative adversarial networks (qGANs) to overcome two critical limitations of early approaches: poor robustness to noise on near-term devices and limited capacity to model complex, multi-modal distributions.

We introduce hybrid qGAN architectures that combine Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty (WGAN-GP) and maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) losses with expressive quantum circuits, including quantum convolutional neural networks (QCNNs) and EfficientSU2 ansätze.
Training is performed using seamless PyTorch–Qiskit integration, enabling stable optimization on both simulators and real quantum hardware.

The management of investment portfolios has become increasingly complex in today's dynamic financial markets, driven by globalization, technological advances, and the growing interconnectedness of financial systems.

The evolution of portfolio optimization traces back to Markowitz's seminal 1952 paper introducing Modern Portfolio Theory (MPT) [1], which established the mathematical framework for portfolio selection based on the mean-variance optimization principle.
Traditional optimization methods are being supplemented or replaced by advanced analytics techniques that can process large-scale datasets and adapt to changing market conditions in real-time [6].

codes.code_label: Survey scope includes modern analytics and risk
codes.text_span: This study examines the landscape of modern portfolio optimization, from its theoretical foundations to cutting-edge applications in data analytics and machine learning, and aims to provide a comprehensive review of portfolio optimization methodologies, and focuses on the integration of modern data analytics and risk management techniques.

codes.code_label: Special attention to machine learning and alternative data
codes.text_span: Special attention is given to recent developments in machine learning applications, alternative data sources, and computational methods that are reshaping portfolio management practices [7].
MPT demonstrates how rational investors can optimize their portfolios by considering both expected returns and risk, measured by variance.

codes.code_label: CAPM links systematic risk to return
codes.text_span: CAPM introduces beta as a measure of systematic risk and suggests that expected return should be proportional to non-diversifiable risk.
APT acknowledges that various macroeconomic factors and market indices can influence asset returns, providing a more comprehensive framework for understanding risk premiums.
Mean-variance optimization, the cornerstone of traditional approaches, implements Markowitz's efficient frontier theory by maximizing expected portfolio return for a given level of risk.
The Black-Litterman model addresses key limitations of mean-variance optimization by incorporating investor views and market equilibrium returns [6].

codes.code_label: Black-Litterman more practical than pure mean-variance
